items.text: Correction of last time
The embedding of a monoid $G$ of finite type is into the monoid $M_n$ of $n\times n$ matrices (multiplication of matrices), not into $\mathrm{GL}_n$; for a group, into $\mathrm{GL}_n$.

$M\subset A$ of finite type generating $A$ as algebra, enlarged so that $\pi(M)\subset M\otimes M$ (so $\pi(M)\subset M\otimes A$): $G$ acts on $M$ on the left (restriction of the regular representation, $A$ = functions on $G$).
\rho\colon G\to\underline{\operatorname{End}}(M)\simeq M_n\quad(\text{not into }\mathrm{GL}(M))
The map $B\to A$ is onto
$B=k[\operatorname{End}M]$. For $x\in M$ define a function $i(x)$ on $\operatorname{End}(M)$: for $u$ an endomorphism of $M_{k'}$,
i(x)(u)=\bigl(u(x)\bigr)(1)\qquad(u(x)\in M_{k'}\subset A_{k'}\ \text{a function on }G_{k'},\ \text{evaluated at the unit})
u=\rho(g):\quad i(x)(\rho(g))=(g\cdot x)(1)=x(g\cdot1)=x(g)
So $i(x)\circ\rho=x$: every $x\in M$ is in the image of $B\to A$; $M$ generates $A$, so $B\to A$ is surjective — a closed immersion.
Monomorphisms of monoids
A monomorphism of a monoid into a group functor: left and right translations act injectively (simplification law).

Fact (only proof known to him is arithmetic: reduce to finite type over $\mathbb Z$, then over a finite field, Artin rings). A monomorphism $X\to X$ of a scheme of finite presentation is an isomorphism.

Consequence: a monoid of finite presentation which embeds in a group functor is already a group: translation by $g\in M(k')$ is a monomorphism $M_{k'}\to M_{k'}$ of finite presentation, hence an isomorphism.
Counterexample: $\mathcal O^{\bullet}\colon k'\mapsto(k',\times)$ does not embed in a group (not every element invertible). Exercise.
Finiteness hypotheses are needed; the same statement for a radicial morphism fails ($t\mapsto t^n$ on $\mathbb G_m$-type examples, an endomorphism that is injective on points but not an isomorphism).
Distributions on an affine space
$X\leftrightarrow A$:
\underline{\operatorname{Dist}}(X)=V(A)\colon k'\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_k(A,k')=\operatorname{Hom}_{k'}(A_{k'},k'),\qquad\text{represented by }S_k(A)
\operatorname{Dist}(X)=\underline{\operatorname{Dist}}(X)(k)=A^{\vee}
Covariant in $X$: $X\to Y$ gives $B\to A$, hence $V(A)\to V(B)$.
V(A)\times V(B)\longrightarrow V(A\otimes B),\qquad (u,v)\mapsto u\boxtimes v=\bigl((A\otimes B)_{k'}\xrightarrow{u\otimes v}k'\otimes k'\to k'\bigr)
$V(A\otimes B)\ne V(A)\otimes V(B)$ in general (equality only if $A$ or $B$ is projective of finite type); the pairing is universal for pairings into some $V(N)$:
V(A\otimes B)=V(A)\boxtimes V(B),\qquad \underline{\operatorname{Dist}}(X\times Y)=\underline{\operatorname{Dist}}(X)\boxtimes\underline{\operatorname{Dist}}(Y)
X\hookrightarrow\underline{\operatorname{Dist}}(X),\qquad X(k')=\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(A,k')\subset\operatorname{Hom}_k(A,k')
The algebra structure $A\otimes A\to A$ gives a diagonal $V(A)\to V(A)\boxtimes V(A)$, i.e. $\underline{\operatorname{Dist}}(X)\to\underline{\operatorname{Dist}}(X\times X)$ (from $X\to X\times X$).
\begin{CD} X @>>> \underline{\operatorname{Dist}}(X)\\ @VVV @VVV\\ X\times X @>>> \underline{\operatorname{Dist}}(X\times X) \end{CD}
An algebra structure on $A$ = a coalgebra structure on $V(A)$ (dual of the earlier statement).
